posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md:
As Joe noted in another thread, the inexpensive digital hygrometers available at local US stores fail permanently when taken to RH < 20%

I've purchased some Timex analog therm/hygrometers that turn out not to work at all.

Can anyone recommend some not too expensive hygrometers or combination thermometer hygrometers? It'd be ideal if they were digital and had a min/max memory.

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
I just bought a pair of these, and I'm very happy with them:

[http://www.iallergy.com/product155/prod ... 2db29dfd25](http://www.iallergy.com/product155/product_info.html?osCsid=2ef29b33d5bf92a6fc8c652db29dfd25) 

There is good agreement between the two for both temperature and humidity. I wouldn't take the RH down too far with these either, as I would imagine they would be damaged also.

posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md: How far down the RH range have you taken them?

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md: Just to the lowest ambient level in my lab, which has been around 39%. Actually, the manual says, quote "Humidity measuring range: 10 - 99% with 1% resolution" I would take this with a grain of salt. With my other meter, I held it at 20% for a prolonged time period, which damaged it. I would think it likely that both use the same or similar technology. It may be tough to find something cheap, reliable, and accurate for really low readings.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md: OK, this is a little strange but it just might work. Take some 1/4 sawn soft wood like spruce. A piece left over from a guitar top would be perfect. Take one piece about 8" long and 1" wide and cut across the grain then glue it to a piece 8" x 1" cut along the grain. Attach one end and let the other end flex. You will have to calibrate it with a sling psycrometer to make it accurate. I find them to be very consistant and not damaged by humidity swings. I used to make them often for guitar making. I found them to be much better than digital or hair driven hydrometers. Second to only sling psycrometers.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md: I should have mentioned that the wood should be about 1/8" thick.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
Right I was giving directions for a *hygrometer*. 

If you go to a homebrew shop to get a hydrometer make sure it is a distillers hydrometer. Beer is heaver than water so the lowest specific gravity on a brewing hydrometer is 1.000. Alcohol and water alone is below 1.000. 

Google this:

Proof and Tralle Hydrometer

Northern Brewer has one for around $8. But lots of suppliers have them now.

As far as a *hygrometer* goes, do you still want one?
